We have mass spec peak at 179.0946 (M+?). That suggests molecular weight ~179.09. The formula we derived from isomers list: C10H13NO2 has exact mass? Let's calculate: C10 = 120.0, H13 = 13.101, N = 14.003, O2 = 31.998 => total ~179.102. Indeed matches 179.0946 (close). So formula C10H13NO2.

Carbon NMR peaks: 166.40 (likely carbonyl C=O), aromatic carbons around 129-132 (multiple), plus 52.24 (maybe O-CH2), 43.47, 38.60 (aliphatic). So structure likely contains an amide carbonyl (C=O at 166 ppm) attached to N, plus aromatic ring (6 carbons). Additional carbons: O-CH2 (52 ppm), maybe CH2 attached to N (43), and a CH (38). The formula C10H13NO2: aromatic ring (C6H4?) plus substituents.

Potential candidates from isomers list: "COC1C(COC2=CC=CC=C12)N" is a benzodioxane? Let's decode: OCH3? Actually SMILES: C O C1 C( C O C2=CC=CC=C12) N . That's a benzoxazine? Contains OCH3 attached to carbon? Let's compute formula: we already saw it's C10H13NO2. Contains carbonyl? No carbonyl present. So carbonyl at 166 ppm not present. So not correct.

Second isomer: "C1C(CO1)C2=CC=C(C=C2)CNO". This is a benzyl alcohol fused? Contains CNO (maybe -CH2-NO?). Contains N-O? Not carbonyl.

We need amide carbonyl. Look at other isomers: "CC(=O)OCCNC1=CC=CC=C1" is an acetamide? Actually CC(=O)OCCN... That's an ester (acetate) plus amine attached to phenyl. Contains carbonyl (ester) at 166 ppm maybe. Formula? Let's compute: CC(=O)OCCN C6H5. That's C? Count: CC(=O)O = C2H3O2? Actually CH3-CO-O-CH2-CH2-N-Ph. Carbons: CH3 (1), carbonyl C (1), OCH2 (1), CH2 (1), phenyl (6) =10. Hydrogens: CH3 (3), OCH2 (2), CH2 (2), phenyl (5), N-H? maybe one H on N (1) =13. N1 O2. So matches C10H13NO2. Good. Carbonyl is ester (166 ppm). Aromatic carbons ~129. OCH2 at 52 ppm (makes sense). CH2 attached to N at 38-43 ppm. So this fits.

Thus likely structure is phenethyl acetate? Actually it's phenethyl carbamate? Wait: CC(=O)OCCNC1=CC=CC=C1 is phenethyl carbamate? Let's parse: CC(=O)O is acetyl group attached to O (acetate). Then CCN attaches to phenyl. So it's 2-(phenylamino)ethyl acetate? Actually O-CH2-CH2-NH-Ph. So it's phenethyl carbamate? Not exactly.

SMILES we validated earlier: "CC(=O)OCCNC1=CC=CC=C1". This is valid.

Check carbon NMR: carbonyl 166.4 matches ester carbonyl. Aromatic carbons 6 signals around 129-132 (makes sense). OCH2 (52.24) matches O-CH2. CH2 attached to N (38.6) matches. The other aliphatic carbon maybe the carbonyl carbon (166) and maybe the CH3 of acetate (should be around 20-30 ppm, but we have 43.47 maybe CH3? Actually CH3 of acetate appears ~20 ppm. But we have 43.47 maybe N-CH2? Wait we already have CH2 at 38.6. 43.47 could be CH3? But CH3 attached to carbonyl (acetyl) appears ~20-30. 43 seems high. Could be N-CH3? But there is no N-CH3. Hmm.

But maybe the 43.47 is the carbonyl carbon? No carbonyl is 166. So 43 could be CH2 next to carbonyl (O-CH2-CH2). Actually O-CH2 attached to carbonyl carbon (acetate) is O-CH2-CH2-N. The carbon directly attached to carbonyl is the O-CH2 (the carbon of the acetate side chain). That carbon is attached to O and carbonyl, chemical shift ~60 ppm. But we have 52.24 for O-CH2 (makes sense). The next CH2 attached to N is ~40 ppm (38.6). So 43.47 maybe the CH3 of acetate (methyl). Methyl attached to carbonyl appears ~20-30, but maybe due to being attached to O? Actually CH3-CO-O- is acetyl methyl, typical shift ~20-30. 43 seems high. Could be the carbonyl carbon of amide? But we have only ester carbonyl.

Maybe the 43.47 is the carbon attached to N (C attached to N and aromatic). Wait N attached to phenyl (aniline). The carbon attached to N is aromatic carbon (ipso) maybe shift ~130. Already accounted.

Thus maybe the 43.47 is the carbon of the carbonyl carbon? No.

Nevertheless the pattern fits.

Let's also get proton NMR to confirm.
